articles.title: Cross-excitation in dorsal root ganglia redistributes coding capacity from stimulus intensity to stimulus location
articles.content: The phenomenon of cross-excitation between neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) of mammals is widely known, yet its exact mechanism remains underexplored. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon as part of the signal processing performed by the body's somatosensory system. We argue that, if the mechanism is indeed as prevalent as it is reported in experimental works, it should provide a significant computational advantage. Here, we created a model network in which sensory A-type neurons are interconnected only via a chemical agent and showed that such a connection, when fitted with parameters similar to those observed in experiments, improves the stimulus-localization properties of the ganglia at the expense of intensity-encoding accuracy. Although this exchange is near-neutral in raw bits, it becomes favorable once the logarithmic compression of intensity perception - the Weber--Fechner law - is taken into account, since the sacrificed intensity capacity is largely perceptually redundant. We therefore propose that cross-excitation is not an imperfection of somatic isolation but an effective, chemically mediated pre-processing stage that sharpens spatial localization.
articles.author: Perevozniuk, D., Koshev, N., Musienko, P.

articles.title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
articles.content: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.
articles.author: Ip, E. Y. J., Igoe, A., Cowan, B. R., Di Liberto, G. M.

articles.title: Extended Pavlovian conditioned approach training and devaluation in Long-Evans rats using time-restricted feeding
articles.content: Pavlovian conditioned approach (PCA) is a useful tool in studying compulsive- and addictive-like behaviors. PCA pairs a cue with reward delivery and rats typically differentiate into three phenotypes (sign-trackers, goal-trackers, and intermediates) based on behavior during the reward-paired cue presentation. Sign-trackers, who preferentially interact with the cue, are more likely to engage in compulsive behaviors and have decreased behavioral flexibility compared to goal-trackers, who preferentially interact with the food cup. However, one limitation to PCA is the use of food deprivation conditions that maintain rats at 80-90% of ad libitum weight, likely increasing stress which may bias animals towards sign-tracking behavior. Furthermore, most behavioral analysis only examines lever pressing and food cup entry, overlooking other behaviors that may better define phenotypes. In the current study male and female Long-Evans rats underwent an extended PCA training paradigm followed by satiety-induced reward devaluation under time-restricted feeding (TRF) conditions. Under TRF, rats continued to gain weight across PCA training and maintained caloric intake relative to ad libitum intake. Expanding the scope of behavioral analysis increased the proportion of ST rats in both early and late PCA training. Rats also increased the time spent interacting with the food cup during the inter-trial interval across extended PCA training. All rats were sensitive to satiety-induced reward devaluation, regardless of sex or devaluation condition. This study helps establish a PCA method optimized for Long-Evans rats with relevance for identifying PCA phenotypes contribution to dysregulated behavior in the context of chronic stress and obesity.
articles.author: Rainer, I. L., Brooks, K., Ulrich-Lai, Y. M., McReynolds, J. R.

articles.title: Walking delays auditory processing in humans alongside a global shift in aperiodic neural activity
articles.content: Natural sensory processing unfolds during movement, yet human electrophysiology is usually measured under enforced stillness. Here, we used mobile EEG to test whether walking changes the timing of auditory processing. Thirty adults listened to lateralised pure tones while walking freely or standing. Walking led to a delay in auditory N1 latency (< 10 ms). Control analyses ruled out the possibility that the N1 delay was contaminated by foot strike related noise in EEG. Multivariate decoding further indicated a later emergence of sound location information during walking in the subset of participants with reliable decoding in both states. Walking also produced a scalp wide decrease in the aperiodic exponent of neural responses. A larger global exponent decrease was associated with a larger N1 delay across participants. Together, these findings show that natural walking reorganises the temporal dynamics of human auditory processing and link early sensory slowing to a global change in ongoing cortical state.
articles.author: Chen, X., Chen, S., Zhang, X., Cao, L.

articles.title: Neonatal NMDA receptor blockade disrupts prefrontal cortical regulation of social affective behavior: implications for schizophrenia
articles.content: Developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr) hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, including cognitive and emotional deficits. However, the neural circuit mechanisms linking developmental NMDAr hypofunction to social affective impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated schizophrenia-related social affective dysfunction induced by neonatal exposure to the NMDAr antagonist MK-801 and examined the contribution of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a key hub for socio-cognitive function. Sprague-Dawley rat pups received subcutaneous injections of saline or MK-801 (MK-Low: 0.2 mg/kg; MK-High: 0.4 mg/kg) during the neonatal period. In adulthood, social affective behaviors were assessed using the Social Affective Preference (SAP) and Social Interaction (SI) tests. MK-801-treated rats, particularly the MK-High group, displayed impaired social affective responses, characterized by reduced preference for and investigation of distressed conspecifics. These impairments were ameliorated by chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal cells in the mPFC, whereas activation of these neurons disrupted social affective behavior in naive rats. Histological analyses revealed reduced parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PVIN) density in the mPFC of MK-801-treated rats. Consistent with the involvement of PVIN dysfunction, selective activation of mPFC PVINs alleviated social affective deficits in MK-801-treated rats. These findings identify impaired PVIN-mediated inhibitory regulation within the mPFC as a circuit mechanism underlying social affective dysfunction following neonatal NMDAr blockade, providing insight into the pathophysiology of schizophrenia-related social impairments.
articles.author: Tachihara, R., Hayashi, N., Rosal, C. G. d., Xiong, T., Igarashi, K., Ozawa, T., Hori, M., Yamada, K., Toyoshima, M.

articles.title: A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
articles.content: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.
articles.author: Lyu, T., Jbabdi, S., Finney, S. M., Clarke, W. T.

articles.title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
articles.content: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.
articles.author: Makarova, J., Munoz-Arnaiz, R., Ashouri, F., Herreras, O.

articles.title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
articles.content: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.
